stem: Written as a product of its prime factors, $1176 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 7^2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain why $6 \times 1176$ is a perfect square.
parts.answer: $6 \times 1176 = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 7^2 = (2^2 \times 3 \times 7)^2 = 84^2$; every prime has an even index, so it is a perfect square.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the smallest positive integer $n$ such that $\frac{1176}{n}$ is a cube number.

solution:
(a) $6 \times 1176 = 2 \times 3 \times 2^3 \times 3 \times 7^2 = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 7^2$.
Every prime factor now has an even index, so $6 \times 1176 = (2^2 \times 3 \times 7)^2 = 84^2$, which is a perfect square.

(b) For $\frac{1176}{n}$ to be a cube number, every prime in its factorisation must have an index that is a multiple of 3.
$1176 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 7^2$: the index of 2 is already 3, so the factors $3$ and $7^2$ must be divided out.
Smallest $n = 3 \times 7^2 = 147$, giving $\frac{1176}{147} = 2^3 = 8$, a cube number.
syllabus_check: 4052 Numbers and their operations: prime factorisation, perfect squares and cubes. Two one-mark parts, one idea each (an explain-why with a number in it, then a smallest-n). Calculator allowed; the factorisation is printed so the skill tested is reasoning on indices, not division.
originality_note: Not a re-skin of any exemplar: the exemplars find x and y, multiply by the smallest k to make a cube, recover N from an HCF/LCM pair, or divide by a prime q. Here the candidate justifies that a given multiple is a square (new number 1176, new multiplier 6) and then finds the smallest DIVISOR that leaves a cube — the division direction with a composite answer, which none of the exemplars ask.
